claims.text: Increasing the quenching rate during reduction limits atomic diffusion and mobility.
Limited atomic mobility freezes the nascent elemental distribution before atoms can migrate and segregate.
Rapid quenching promotes formation of homogeneous, single-phase noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Rapid quenching promotes nanoparticles with high surface-atom exposure.
Slower quenching permits enough atomic mobility to cause phase segregation or elemental clustering.
The proposed initial material is a homogeneous mixture of more than five noble-metal precursors in a single-source formulation adsorbed on a support.
Using a solid, mixed single-source precursor provides limited diffusion pathways or limited free-atom mobility.
The controlled comparison changes cooling rate while holding precursor composition, heating rate, peak temperature, reduction conditions, and atmosphere constant.
The relevant structural mediator is the extent of atomic mobility or diffusion during particle formation.
When atom generation or deposition outpaces surface diffusion, solid-solution high-entropy alloy nanocrystals can form.
Under limited free-atom mobility, increasing the number of atom types increases the likelihood of forming a random alloy.
Faster quenching will produce more homogeneous single-phase particles than slower quenching.
Slower-quenching samples will show detectably greater phase separation or elemental segregation than rapid-quenching samples.
A moderate-quenching baseline exhibits partial homogenization together with some elemental ordering or segregation.
The mechanism applies to noble metal-based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles made from single-source precursors under rapid reduction conditions.
The mechanism may not apply to solution-phase, ligand-dominated, or fundamentally different reduction chemistries.
Differences in elemental redox potentials and precursor chemistry can alter reduction timing and complicate a simple diffusion-versus-reduction-rate model.
The quantitative quenching-rate threshold required to freeze the atomic arrangement is unknown.
A lack of statistically significant phase-homogeneity or segregation differences between slow- and rapid-quenching samples would falsify quenching rate as the key controlling parameter.

contradictions.description: The initial state calls for more than five noble-metal precursors, but its example lists exactly five elements (Pt, Pd, Fe, Co, and Ni), and Fe, Co, and Ni are not ordinarily classified as noble metals. This makes the stated composition class internally inconsistent.
